learningObjective: Classify domain concepts from explicit identity, continuity, equality, and lifecycle facts, and place a domain operation where the required decision spans concepts.

question.prompt: A rights-clearance tool tracks each approved usage by a clearance number because an approval can be suspended or renewed while its territory and expiry values change. Two approvals may have identical territory and expiry but remain separately auditable. How should the model treat an approval?

options.text: Keep the clearance ID; treat territory and expiry as changeable values.
Treat the territory-and-expiry pair as the approval identity, merging approvals whose fields happen to match.
Keep approval as a stateless calculation result rather than a retained record.

feedback.reason: The clearance number and audit history distinguish approvals even when descriptive fields match; territory and expiry can change without replacing that approval identity.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Clearance identity continues across amendments; territory and expiry values describe its current authorized scope.
details.scenarioApplication: The clearance number remains the review team’s reference while territory and expiry describe the currently approved use.
details.errorCorrection: Equal descriptive fields do not make separately auditable approval records the same approval. The approval has a retained identity and lifecycle, so a transient calculation alone loses required history.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A context that only displays current territory/expiry may use a value snapshot; the approval record still has identity here.
details.transfer: Use the scenario’s continuity and audit facts to decide identity; matching fields alone do not settle whether two records are the same.

messages.text: Equal descriptive fields do not make separately auditable approval records the same approval.
The approval has a retained identity and lifecycle, so a transient calculation alone loses required history.

question.prompt: A drone fleet records each battery by serial number through installation, removal, repair, and retirement. Charge percentage is a current measurement, not an identifier; two batteries can show the same percentage. Which model distinction fits?

options.text: Treat charge percentage as battery identity and serial as display metadata.
Key the battery by serial; treat charge as a changing measurement.
Treat battery and charge as one immutable value, making a new battery record for every reading.

feedback.reason: Serial continuity follows the physical battery through lifecycle changes, while charge readings vary and can match across units.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Serial identity follows the physical battery through repair and retirement; charge percentage is a repeated, changing observation.
details.scenarioApplication: Repair and retirement history follows the same serial-numbered battery while charge readings vary over time.
details.errorCorrection: A changing, nonunique measurement cannot identify which physical battery is being repaired or retired. Replacing battery identity on every reading would erase the continuity the lifecycle requires.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A historical reading can itself be an immutable value record if timestamped; the battery remains the continuing entity.
details.transfer: Separate the thing whose identity persists from values that describe it at a particular observation.

messages.text: A changing, nonunique measurement cannot identify which physical battery is being repaired or retired.
Replacing battery identity on every reading would erase the continuity the lifecycle requires.

question.prompt: A referral is tracked by referral ID from creation through routing and closure. Consent is a signed record with its own ID and revocation history; the requested specialty code is selected from a catalog. Which modeling choice preserves these facts?

options.text: Make specialty the referral identity and store consent as a boolean without separate history.
Flatten referral, consent, and specialty into one immutable tuple recreated whenever routing changes.
Keep referral and consent identities separate; specialty is a value.

feedback.reason: The referral and consent each have their own lifecycles and audit identity; specialty is a catalog value that describes the referral.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Referral and consent each have independent identity/history, while a shared specialty code describes routing.
details.scenarioApplication: Separate referral and consent histories stay auditable even when multiple referrals share a specialty code.
details.errorCorrection: A specialty can be shared by many referrals and does not identify one referral or consent history. A single immutable tuple obscures independently changing referral and revocation histories.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A routing view may project consent status and specialty together without erasing underlying identities.
details.transfer: Model independent lifecycles as distinct concepts; use values for shared descriptors that carry no separate continuity.

messages.text: A specialty can be shared by many referrals and does not identify one referral or consent history.
A single immutable tuple obscures independently changing referral and revocation histories.

question.prompt: A practice tracker stores each published exercise revision by ID. Each completion points to that revision and the scoring-policy version used at the time; two revisions may display the same title. What should define a completed exercise’s association?

options.text: Reference the exact exercise revision and scoring-policy version from completion, despite later reuse of the title.
Use the displayed title, with completion always resolving to whichever revision currently has that title.
Copy only title and score, dropping revision and policy references after grading.

feedback.reason: The completion must be interpretable against the exact revision and policy that produced it; title equality does not establish version equality.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A completion’s exact revision and policy references preserve the meaning of its recorded score despite title reuse.
details.scenarioApplication: A completed score remains attributable to revision 8 and policy 3 even if a later exercise reuses the title.
details.errorCorrection: The premise allows multiple revisions with the same title, so title cannot resolve which content was completed. Dropping version references makes historical scores ambiguous under later revisions.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A display layer can show the current title while retaining immutable revision and policy associations.
details.transfer: When history must remain explainable, retain the identities or versions that gave the result its meaning.

messages.text: The premise allows multiple revisions with the same title, so title cannot resolve which content was completed.
Dropping version references makes historical scores ambiguous under later revisions.

question.prompt: An exception request has a request ID, amount and scope that may be amended before review, and a final decision by a named approver. Each amendment remains in the audit trail. Which model best represents it?

options.text: An immutable value made only from amount and scope; discard earlier amendments when fields change.
Keep request identity and amendment history; record the approver decision.
A single approval service object whose in-memory fields are the only record of the decision.

feedback.reason: The request survives edits under one auditable identity, while the decision is a recorded outcome rather than mutable service state.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The request identity preserves amendment lineage, and the named approver’s decision is a retained outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Reviewers can trace edits to the request and identify the approver’s final decision.
details.errorCorrection: Replacing the value would lose the amendment history required by the scenario. An in-memory coordinator is not the durable request/decision record the facts call for.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An application service can coordinate review without becoming the domain record or sole home of approval history.
details.transfer: Choose identity for continuity across edits and model recorded decisions where audit facts require them; keep orchestration separate.

messages.text: Replacing the value would lose the amendment history required by the scenario.
An in-memory coordinator is not the durable request/decision record the facts call for.

question.prompt: An annotation follows a stable segment ID across recording replacements. Two annotations can contain the same text but remain separate because authors and creation records differ. Which representation is appropriate?

options.text: Use annotation text as identity and merge records whenever their words match.
Identify annotation by recording byte offset and rewrite identity when the recording changes.
Keep annotation identity with its author and stable segment; treat annotation text as editable content.

feedback.reason: The annotation has an individual authoring history and follows a stable segment; content and file location are not its identity.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Annotation authorship persists independently of editable text and recording offsets; stable segment identity supplies the reference.
details.scenarioApplication: After a recording changes, authorship and the segment link persist even when annotation text is edited.
details.errorCorrection: Identical text can represent two different authored notes under the stated facts. Byte offsets change during replacement and contradict the stable-segment association.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Text can be compared or edited as data while the annotation record’s continuity remains separate.
details.transfer: Do not use mutable or nonunique attributes as identity when the scenario supplies a stable lifecycle key.

messages.text: Identical text can represent two different authored notes under the stated facts.
Byte offsets change during replacement and contradict the stable-segment association.

question.prompt: A role grant has a grant ID, expiry, and approval reference. Role name is chosen from a shared list and may be corrected without replacing the grant. How should these concepts be modeled?

options.text: Give the grant its own ID and lifecycle; use role name as a reusable value.
Treat role name as grant identity and overwrite any prior grant for that role.
Treat the complete grant as an untracked value recreated whenever expiry is adjusted.

feedback.reason: A grant has its own attributable lifecycle and can be amended, while role name is a reusable classification value.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The grant has its own approval-backed lifecycle; a shared role label classifies the authorization but does not identify it.
details.scenarioApplication: The approval and expiry remain tied to one grant even if its shared role label is corrected.
details.errorCorrection: The same role may be granted through separate approvals or to different recipients; its name cannot identify a grant. Recreating an untracked value would lose grant ID and approval relationship.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Role definitions could have their own lifecycle elsewhere; this question concerns an individual grant record.
details.transfer: Keep a lifecycle-bearing authorization record distinct from reusable labels that describe its scope.

messages.text: The same role may be granted through separate approvals or to different recipients; its name cannot identify a grant.
Recreating an untracked value would lose grant ID and approval relationship.

question.prompt: A notary records each seal by seal ID, signer, and timestamp. The signed revision is immutable and identified by a content digest; several seals may reference the same revision. Which distinction is sound?

options.text: Use revision digest as seal identity so later seals replace earlier ones.
Keep each seal ID separate from the revision digest it targets.
Copy the document into a new mutable document entity for every signature.

feedback.reason: Separate seal records remain auditable even for the same revision; the digest identifies immutable content being sealed.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Each seal is a distinct recorded act; the digest identifies its immutable target, not the seal event.
details.scenarioApplication: The audit can distinguish two seal records that refer to the same immutable document revision.
details.errorCorrection: Multiple distinct seals may refer to one revision, so the digest cannot identify each seal. The revision is explicitly immutable; per-signature mutable copies confuse the target with the act.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A document repository may have its own identity; the revision value remains fixed for this seal record.
details.transfer: Model an action record with its own identity separately from the immutable value or version it acts on.

messages.text: Multiple distinct seals may refer to one revision, so the digest cannot identify each seal.
The revision is explicitly immutable; per-signature mutable copies confuse the target with the act.

question.prompt: A payout has a payout ID and transitions from proposed to released. Its money amount consists of currency and minor units, and equal amounts can belong to different sellers. Which model follows the domain facts?

options.text: Use amount as payout ID so equal amounts collapse into one payment.
Let the release service request object be the only payout record and discard it after sending.
Keep payout ID for lifecycle; represent money as currency and amount.

feedback.reason: Payout lifecycle and seller association persist under its ID; money compares as a value but cannot distinguish payouts.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Payout ID follows the release lifecycle; currency and amount are comparable values that can repeat across sellers.
details.scenarioApplication: Two sellers with equal monetary values still have separate payout IDs and release histories.
details.errorCorrection: Two sellers may receive equal amounts while retaining different payout histories. Discarding the request removes the identity and release state the scenario requires.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A service can invoke release, but a retained payout record still tracks its lifecycle.
details.transfer: Identify the lifecycle-bearing record first; represent quantities with their units and keep command coordination distinct.

messages.text: Two sellers may receive equal amounts while retaining different payout histories.
Discarding the request removes the identity and release state the scenario requires.

question.prompt: A disruption board records each platform-change notice by notice ID and effective time. Platform code is selected from a station list; corrections create a superseding notice while preserving the earlier notice. What is the right modeling choice?

options.text: Keep notice identity/history; treat platform and time as attributes.
Treat platform code plus time as notice identity and overwrite an earlier notice with the same pair.
Treat each passenger notification as the domain notice and discard the controller’s accepted change record.

feedback.reason: The notice has retained identity and correction history; platform and time are attributes that can repeat across notices.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A notice and its correction history continue independently of platform code and effective-time attributes.
details.scenarioApplication: A correction to one platform notice can be traced without overwriting another notice’s event history.
details.errorCorrection: Overwriting destroys the preserved earlier notice and assumes descriptive values uniquely identify the event. Passenger delivery is a consequence, not the accepted change record the controller manages.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A delivery message may have its own retry ID, separate from the domain notice identity.
details.transfer: Distinguish the business event record from its descriptive values and downstream communications.

messages.text: Overwriting destroys the preserved earlier notice and assumes descriptive values uniquely identify the event.
Passenger delivery is a consequence, not the accepted change record the controller manages.

question.prompt: A meter reservation selects a meter and time interval. Each confirmed reservation has its own ID and can be cancelled independently; interval equality is determined by start/end instants regardless of formatting. Which distinction fits?

options.text: Use interval as reservation identity and merge requests with equal start/end.
Track cancellation by reservation ID; compare intervals by normalized start and end instants, not formatting.
Treat formatted time string as identity and let equivalent formats create separate windows.

feedback.reason: Independent cancellation requires reservation identity, while normalized endpoints define the interval value for comparison.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Reservations cancel independently by ID; interval equality compares normalized instants rather than textual formatting.
details.scenarioApplication: Equivalent time formats compare as the same interval while separate requests remain independently cancellable.
details.errorCorrection: Two customers’ reservations may have identical intervals but remain separate requests with separate histories. Formatting differences do not change the instants and should not create distinct intervals.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The meter may also have a lifecycle identity; interval comparison remains a value-level rule.
details.transfer: Use identity for independently managed records and canonical value equality for measurements or intervals.

messages.text: Two customers’ reservations may have identical intervals but remain separate requests with separate histories.
Formatting differences do not change the instants and should not create distinct intervals.

question.prompt: A caption stream session has a session ID and history of provider changes. A provider configuration consists of endpoint, language, and timing parameters; replacing those values does not create a new stream session. Which model is appropriate?

options.text: Use endpoint string as session identity and create a new session whenever timing changes.
Make provider configuration the sole domain record and discard session change history.
Preserve the stream session ID and provider-change history while endpoint, language, and timing settings change.

feedback.reason: The session continues across provider changes; configuration values describe how that session is served at a point in time.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The stream session continues across provider changes; configuration values describe successive operating choices.
details.scenarioApplication: The session history remains one stream identity as endpoint and timing configuration change.
details.errorCorrection: An endpoint may be shared across sessions and can change without changing session identity. Removing the session record loses the provider-change history required by the scenario.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A provider resource could have its own lifecycle; it does not replace the running session identity.
details.transfer: Separate a continuing process identity from replaceable configuration snapshots.

messages.text: An endpoint may be shared across sessions and can change without changing session identity.
Removing the session record loses the provider-change history required by the scenario.

question.prompt: A volunteer shift contains two separately identified assignments. A swap must check both volunteers’ skill and availability; neither assignment alone can make that decision. What should the model use for the swap decision?

options.text: Evaluate the swap across both assignment records, then change both.
Put scheduling behavior in the volunteer name value so each volunteer decides independently.
Make one assignment inherit from the other so the pair can share a swap method.

feedback.reason: The decision spans two independent assignment identities and compares facts about both volunteers; an operation can coordinate without collapsing those entities.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The swap needs facts from two independent assignments, so the decision spans records without turning them into a subtype relation.
details.scenarioApplication: The swap decision compares both assignments’ volunteer skill and availability facts.
details.errorCorrection: A display name neither owns availability nor represents the two-assignment decision. Inheritance models a subtype relationship, not a temporary relationship between two assignments.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Each assignment can guard local facts; the cross-assignment decision needs information from both.
details.transfer: Place an operation where all required decision facts are visible while retaining the identities it coordinates.

messages.text: A display name neither owns availability nor represents the two-assignment decision.
Inheritance models a subtype relationship, not a temporary relationship between two assignments.

question.prompt: An offline route edit has an edit ID and parent route revision. Its geometry is proposed content that can be revised before acceptance; after acceptance, a new route revision gets a new identity. How should the domain distinguish these records?

options.text: Use geometry equality as edit identity and merge identical shapes from different authors.
Keep edit ID and parent revision; treat geometry as proposed content.
Treat each geometry point as an independent route entity and discard edit-level history.

feedback.reason: The proposal has authorship and parentage across revisions; geometry is the content being evaluated, not enough to identify its history.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The edit ID and parent revision preserve proposal lineage; geometry is content that can be revised or compared.
details.scenarioApplication: Before acceptance, proposed geometry remains an edit linked to its parent revision rather than a new route revision.
details.errorCorrection: Identical geometry can arise from separate edits and does not erase author or parent-revision facts. Point records do not preserve edit-level conflict and lineage.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Accepted route revisions can have durable identities; an unaccepted edit remains a separate proposal.
details.transfer: Keep change proposals and lineage identifiable, while treating proposed structure as content subject to comparison.

messages.text: Identical geometry can arise from separate edits and does not erase author or parent-revision facts.
Point records do not preserve edit-level conflict and lineage.

question.prompt: A campaign defines reward rules by version. Each claim stores which rule version was applied; a point bundle is a set of categories and quantities. A later rule revision must not rewrite old claims. Which representation is best?

options.text: Use point bundle as rule identity and update old claims when a quantity changes.
Store the applied rule only in the reward service’s current configuration.
Give each claim its applied rule-version reference and capture the point categories and quantities as values.

feedback.reason: Claims refer to a specific versioned rule, and the captured bundle describes granted values without replacing claim or rule identity.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Rule versions and claims need history, while the point bundle records the values applied by one claim.
details.scenarioApplication: A claim can reconstruct the rule version applied while retaining the exact point bundle it granted.
details.errorCorrection: Different rules can grant the same bundle, and changing it must not rewrite historical claims. Current service configuration cannot explain which rule a past claim used.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A rule catalog may have a separate lifecycle, but each claim retains the version it used.
details.transfer: Use identity/version for concepts whose history matters and snapshot values for the exact result applied.

messages.text: Different rules can grant the same bundle, and changing it must not rewrite historical claims.
Current service configuration cannot explain which rule a past claim used.

question.prompt: Dispatch manages shipments with persistent shipment IDs. Carrier choices are independent entities; a temperature band is a pair of inclusive limits. Choosing a carrier compares the shipment band, carrier capability, and hand-off status. What model fits?

options.text: Keep shipment and carrier identities; compare them using band values in an operation.
Make temperature-band value inherit from each carrier and decide assignment by subtype.
Treat carrier name as shipment identity and overwrite shipment history whenever dispatch changes.

feedback.reason: Eligibility depends on facts from two continuing records and a comparable range; it is a domain decision spanning them.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Eligibility combines two identities with a comparable temperature range; no single record contains every decision fact.
details.scenarioApplication: Carrier eligibility combines shipment requirements with a candidate carrier’s capabilities and hand-off status.
details.errorCorrection: A range of limits describes compatibility and does not define a carrier subtype. Changing carrier does not change which shipment is being tracked.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The operation can coordinate dispatch while shipment and carrier retain their identities and local behavior.
details.transfer: Model comparisons across independently identified concepts as an operation when neither alone has all decision facts.

messages.text: A range of limits describes compatibility and does not define a carrier subtype.
Changing carrier does not change which shipment is being tracked.

question.prompt: A repayment is recorded under a transaction ID and can be allocated across several loan accounts. Currency and amount are value data; the allocation rule checks each account’s current balance. Which design is strongest?

options.text: Use repayment amount as transaction identity and merge equal payments across borrowers.
Retain transaction identity across allocations; compare currency/amount values with each loan account’s current balance in the allocation decision.
Put balance-allocation rules in the currency value so money decides which accounts receive it.

feedback.reason: The transaction ID distinguishes a financial event, while amounts are values and allocation needs both repayment and account balances.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Repayment identity records the financial event; allocation compares amount values against multiple account balances.
details.scenarioApplication: Allocating one repayment across accounts uses each account’s balance while preserving one repayment identity.
details.errorCorrection: Equal amounts can be separate payments with different source and borrower histories. Currency has no account balance or allocation context and cannot own this multi-account decision.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An account can enforce its own balance invariant; the operation determines division across accounts.
details.transfer: Separate event identity, dimensional values, and cross-entity decisions instead of forcing all behavior into one concept.

messages.text: Equal amounts can be separate payments with different source and borrower histories.
Currency has no account balance or allocation context and cannot own this multi-account decision.
